questions.problem: Determine the solutions of the equation ${f}^{2}=-25.$
questions.worked_solution:
By taking square root, we obtain:

$$
f=\pm \sqrt{-25}
$$

We now rewrite $f$ using the imaginary unit $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f & =\pm \sqrt{-25} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{25\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{25}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm 5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $8{y}^{2}+12=0?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 8{y}^{2} & =-12 \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{12}{8} \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By taking square root, we obtain:

$$
y=\pm \sqrt{-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

We now rewrite $y$ using the imaginary unit $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \sqrt{-\frac{3}{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\text{i} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Solving a Quadratic Equation With Purely Imaginary Solutions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		x^2 + 16 &= 0 \[3pt]
		x^2 &= -16
}
$$

By taking the square root, we obtain

$$
x = \pm \sqrt{-16}.
$$

We now rewrite $x$ using the imaginary unit $\textrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}\, \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\pm \sqrt{-16} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{16\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{16}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x = \pm 4 \textrm{i}.$

Example: 
                    Solving a Quadratic Equation With Purely Imaginary Solutions With Simplification
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
p^2 + 27 & = 0\[3pt]

p^2 & = -27 
}
$$

By taking the square root, we obtain

$$
p = \pm \sqrt{-27}.
$$

We now rewrite $p$ using the imaginary unit $\textrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}\, \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =\pm \sqrt{-27} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{27\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{27}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{{3}^{2}\cdot 3}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm 3\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm 3\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $p = \pm 3\sqrt{3} \, \textrm{i}.$

Example: 
                    Solving a Quadratic Equation With Purely Imaginary Fractional Solutions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
16z^2 + 49 & = 0\[5pt]

16z^2 & = -49 \[5pt]

z^2 & = -\dfrac{49}{16}
}
$$

By taking the square root, we obtain

$$
z = \pm \sqrt{-\dfrac{49}{16}}.
$$

We now rewrite $z$ using the imaginary unit $\textrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}\, \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\pm \sqrt{-\frac{49}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{49}{16}\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{49}{16}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{49}}{\sqrt{16}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{7}{4}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $z=\pm \dfrac{7}{4} \textrm{i}.$

canonical_examples.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $2y^2 + 9 = 0?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		2y^2 + 9 &= 0 \[5pt]

		2y^2 &= -9\[5pt]

y^2 & = -\dfrac{9}{2}
}
$$

By taking square root, we obtain

$$
y = \pm \sqrt{-\dfrac{9}{2}}.
$$

We now rewrite $y$ using the imaginary unit $\textrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}\, \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \sqrt{-\frac{9}{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{2}\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\text{i} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $y=\pm \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \textrm{i}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When solving an equation, we sometimes require taking the square root of a negative number. In such cases, we will not end up with real solutions, but imaginary solutions.

To demonstrate, let's solve the equation $2x^2 +8 = 0$ for $x.$ First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		2x^2 + 8 &= 0 \[3pt]
		2x^2 &= -8 \[3pt]
		x^2 &= -4
}
$$

By taking the square root, we obtain

$$
x = \pm \sqrt{-4}.
$$

We now rewrite $x$ using the imaginary unit $\textrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}\, \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{4\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x = \pm 2 \textrm{i}.$
